title: Indigenous rainforest peoples: the Yanomami
keyIdea: Indigenous peoples have lived in rainforests for thousands of years, and many still live there today. The Yanomami live in the Amazon rainforest in Brazil and Venezuela. They build big round houses that many families share, from tree poles, vines and palm leaves. Most of their food grows in gardens, and they also gather, hunt and fish. When a garden's soil gets tired after two or three years, they make a new small garden and the old one grows back into forest. They know hundreds of forest plants for food, medicine and building.
familyTip: Look at a globe or map together and find the equator, then the Amazon in South America. Ask: what would you build a house from if you only had the trees around you? At dinner, sort what is on your plates into grown, gathered, or caught.

visual.caption: From the forest or from a factory? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build a round house, sort food, run a moving garden, find rainforest peoples today, and share a catch.

kid: Some people live in the rainforest. Their families have lived there for thousands of years. They still live there today. One group is called the Yanomami. Say it like this: ya-no-MA-mee. They live in the Amazon rainforest in South America.

The Yanomami live in a big round house. Lots of families share it. They build it from tree poles, vines and palm leaves. All of these grow in the forest. The middle of the house is open to the sky. Children play there.

Most of their food grows in a garden. They grow plantains and cassava. They also find wild honey and nuts. They catch fish and hunt wild pigs. A hunter does not eat his own catch. He shares it with other families.

After two or three years, the garden soil gets tired. So they make a new small garden. The old garden grows back into forest. The Yanomami know hundreds of plants. They know which ones are food and which ones are medicine.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. This links KS1 geography (understand the human features of a small area in a contrasting non-European country; hot areas of the world and the equator) with KS1 science (living things and their habitats). Indigenous peoples are the first peoples of a place, who keep their own languages and ways of life. The Yanomami number about 45,000 people in the rainforests and mountains of northern Brazil and southern Venezuela (Survival International). People have lived in the Amazon for more than 10,000 years. Key words: indigenous, rainforest, equator, shelter, garden, gather, hunt, medicine, community.

Yanomami communities live in large round shared houses called yanos or shabonos. Some house up to 400 people, with an open central area for feasts and games. Gardens of around 60 crops, such as plantains and cassava, give about 80% of their food. Hunting gives only about 10%, though meat is highly valued. People also gather nuts, shellfish, insect larvae and 15 kinds of wild honey. No hunter eats the meat he has killed; he shares it out, and others share with him. Amazon soil is not very fertile, so a new garden is cleared every two or three years and the old one grows back. They use about 500 plants for food, medicine and building (Survival International).

Other rainforest peoples include the Baka of the Congo Basin rainforest in Central Africa and the Penan of Borneo in South-East Asia. Their lands are under pressure. Illegal gold mining in Yanomami land has brought pollution and disease, and Yanomami leaders such as Davi Kopenawa speak up for the forest. With young children, keep the focus on how people live and what they know, and use the names that peoples use for themselves.

Common mistakes: thinking rainforest peoples lived only long ago, when many live there today; thinking they live only by hunting, when most food is grown in gardens; thinking a garden means cutting down the whole forest; and thinking all rainforest peoples are one group. In the lab your child builds a round house in order (poles, vines, palm leaves), sorts 6 foods into grow, gather, or hunt and fish, runs a garden for 9 years and watches an old patch grow back, places three peoples on their rainforests, and shares 6 pieces of meat fairly between 3 families.

practice.prompt: What do the Yanomami build their round house from?
choices: Tree poles, vines and palm leaves
practice.hint: Think about the three parts you used in the lab.
practice.explain: The house is made from the forest: poles for the frame, vines to tie them, and palm leaves for the roof.

practice.prompt: A hunter brings home {=3*a} pieces of meat. He shares them fairly between 3 families. How many pieces does each family get?
practice.hint: Give one piece to each family, again and again, until none are left.
practice.explain: {=3*a} pieces shared between 3 families is {a} pieces each. The hunter shares it all.

practice.prompt: A garden is used for 3 years. Then the family makes a new garden. How many years do {a} gardens last, one after the other?
practice.hint: Count on in threes, one jump for each garden.
practice.explain: {a} gardens of 3 years each last {=3*a} years. Each old garden grows back into forest.

practice.prompt: Where does most Yanomami food come from?
practice.explain: Most food is grown in their gardens, like plantains and cassava. Hunting gives only a small part.

practice.prompt: Do people still live in rainforests today?
practice.hint: Think about the Yanomami, the Baka and the Penan.
practice.explain: Yes. The Yanomami, the Baka, the Penan and many other peoples live in rainforests today.

pool.prompt: In which rainforest do the Yanomami live?
choices: A forest at the North Pole
pool.hint: It is the biggest rainforest, in South America.
pool.explain: The Yanomami live in the Amazon rainforest, in Brazil and Venezuela.

pool.prompt: What makes the roof of the round house?
pool.hint: It grows on trees in the forest.
pool.explain: Palm leaves make the roof. Poles make the frame, and vines tie it together.

pool.prompt: {a} families live in one round house. Then {b} more families move in. How many families live there now?
pool.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more.
pool.explain: {a} families and {b} more make {=a+b} families. Many families share one big round house.

pool.prompt: The garden soil is tired. What do the Yanomami do?
pool.hint: What happened to the old garden in the lab?
pool.explain: They make a new small garden. The old garden grows back into forest.

pool.prompt: A hunter catches a wild pig. What does he do with the meat?
pool.hint: Think about the last step of the lab.
pool.explain: A Yanomami hunter does not eat his own catch. He shares it, and other hunters share with him.

pool.prompt: A family finds {a} honeycombs and {b} bags of nuts in the forest. How many things did they gather?
pool.hint: Add the honeycombs and the bags of nuts.
pool.explain: {a} and {b} make {=a+b}. Honey and nuts are gathered in the forest, not grown.

pool.prompt: Which of these do the Yanomami grow in their gardens?
pool.hint: Which food has to be planted?
pool.explain: Plantains and cassava are grown in gardens. Honey is gathered, and fish are caught.

pool.prompt: Who lives in a rainforest in Africa?
pool.hint: Think about the three rainforests in the lab.
pool.explain: The Baka live in the Congo rainforest in Africa. The Yanomami live in the Amazon, and the Penan in Borneo.
